articles.body: The campaign for Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola actively participated in an effort to peel votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by recruiting namesake and spoiler candidates, according to an investigation The New York Times published Wednesday. The covert operation, internally dubbed the "ballot composition project," allegedly involved aides from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), top campaign advisors, party lawyers and an operative who traveled across the state under assumed names. In a series of posts on Truth Social, President Donald Trump said Peltola shouldn't be allowed to keep her name on the ballot, citing the instance as "ELECTION FRAUD." The effort began in the summer of 2025, when a Peltola staffer was directed to comb through state voter rolls to compile a list of Alaskans named Dan Sullivan, according to the report. The plan worked earlier this year when Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher and left-leaning voter from Petersburg, switched his voter registration to Republican shortly before filing his candidacy in the Senate race. TRUMP SAYS 'WE ARE LOOKING INTO' OTHER DAN SULLIVAN ON ALASKA BALLOT, WARNS ABOUT GOVERNOR'S RACE PERSONAL ATTACKS FLY AS SULLIVAN, PELTOLA SPAR OVER CORRUPTION, CHARACTER AND CONTROVERSY Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired in August, told the Times that while Peltola was not directly involved in orchestrating the project, she was "definitely aware." "Alaskan voters need to know," Rios said. "There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions." Rios later attempted to retract her comments prior to publication, but the newspaper noted that her initial interviews were corroborated by text messages, internal documents and 11 other sources. Central to the plan was Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz, who allegedly traveled through Alaska using aliases such as "Zane," the report states. TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY Kurtz allegedly met potential recruits at local pubs and diners, offering outside financial backing to persuade conservative and independent candidates to run and split the right-leaning vote. "The Democrats cheated!" Trump wrote. "They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it. That’s perjury. She shouldn’t be allowed to run, and neither should the FAKE Dan Sullivan!" "Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done, A FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC, and Dan Sullivan should be allowed to run without either Mary Peltola or FAKE Dan Sullivan on the Ballot," he added. Beyond the second Sullivan, operatives recruited other potential candidates, including drywall contractor Gerald Heikes, according to the report. GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING They also allegedly successfully pressured progressive candidate David Leslie to drop out of the race to avoid siphoning votes from Peltola, paving the way for Heikes to claim the fourth spot on Alaska’s ranked-choice ballot. Campaign advisors and the DSCC also weighed creating a third-party "MAGA party" to siphon votes from the incumbent senator before abandoning the idea in May, according to the report. Jacquelyn Lopez, an attorney with the prominent Democratic firm Elias Law Group, which represents both the DSCC and Peltola’s campaign, was looped into discussions regarding the third-party strategy and field operations, the Times wrote. Internal messages allegedly showed staff asking whether they needed to "follow up with Jackie about maga party stuff," while another noted that Lopez was in touch with Kurtz. CLICK HERE FOR MORE U.S. NEWS "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race," Peltola’s campaign said in a statement to the Times. The DSCC echoed that stance, stating it had no role in recruiting either Sullivan or any other Republican candidate. In a statement to Fox News, the DSCC said it was not involved with Dan J. Sullivan, while pointing to Republicans' allegations of political shenanigans. "Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns, including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," a DSCC spokesperson said. The White House pointed to a social media post by Communications Director Steven Cheung on X: "BREAKING: Democrats' secret, CORRUPT plan to stack Alaska's ballot EXPOSED!" Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) said Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn was a “clear winner” in a final debate before the midterm election against Democrat Rob Sand.

“And unlike @RobSandIA, he was unafraid to take a stand for our most vulnerable citizens. I’m proud to support Zach and Iowa First!” the retiring governor wrote in a post on the social platform X .

The candidates clashed in the latest debate on Tuesday hosted by KCRG and The Gazette in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, following two other debates this month on Oct. 6 and Oct. 14.

In dissenting views, Lahn argued in favor of preserving Iowa’s culture, pointing to issues in education as well as his conservative stances on abortion and transgender athletes.

Sand vowed to veto any “culture war” issues and noted Iowa’s six-week abortion ban, calling it “incredibly restrictive.”

“Vetoing culture war bills to me is just a different way to say I want us to put 100 percent of our legislating time into issues that impact 100 percent of Iowans,” he said in a report by The Des Moines Register .

In an earlier debate , the pair sparred on several issues, including jabs surrounding family roots, culture-war issues, and Lahn’s opposition to the COVID-19 vaccine, before finally agreeing on property taxes. Both candidates suggested they preferred localities have more say on taxes.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ , a partner of The Hill, leans toward Sand in the upcoming elections, with a 70 percent possibility of him winning.

articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday said former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) should not be allowed to run for Senate against incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) following a report that her campaign sought to recruit other candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan, in an effort to impact the election results.

“In Alaska, I don’t think Mary Peltola, after perpetrating such a terrible scheme, should be allowed to run, because this is ELECTION FRAUD,” Trump wrote in a post on TruthSocial.

“The Democrats cheated! They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it. That’s perjury. She shouldn’t be allowed to run, and neither should the FAKE Dan Sullivan!” he continued.

Trump also called on Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan to be prosecuted while speaking with reporters on Wednesday.

“I think the fake Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola, number one they should be taken off the ballot, and number two they should be prosecuted,” the president said.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Peltola campaign aides, the campaign’s lawyers and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) staffers were involved in pushing other candidates.

Peltola’s campaign and the DSCC have denied being involved with the effort.

“The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in DC. and did not recruit any candidates into the race,” the Peltola campaign said in a statement.

Despite Trump’s comments, the alleged tactics are not illegal. The New York Times noted they are considered common in politics and have been deployed by Republican and Democratic campaigns.

The development comes after the Justice Department filed a lawsuit to block the state’s Senate contest’s results from being certified if the incumbent loses, citing the two Sullivans on the ballot.

The Peltola campaign has asked the judge to dismiss that case, prompting the judge to expedite the litigation.

Alaska is one of the most contested Senate races this cycle. Trump and Vice President Vance have traveled to the state to campaign with the incumbent senator, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up.

articles.title: Republicans rip Peltola over report her campaign recruited second Sullivan
articles.summary: Republicans are blasting Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola (D) over reports her campaign recruited one of her midterm opponents, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to counter incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R) reelection bid. The New York Times reported Wednesday Peltola’s campaign directly attempted to recruit someone with the same name as her GOP opponent — allegations…
articles.body:
Republicans are blasting Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola (D) over reports her campaign recruited one of her midterm opponents, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to counter incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R) reelection bid.

The New York Times reported Wednesday Peltola’s campaign directly attempted to recruit someone with the same name as her GOP opponent — allegations the former congresswoman denied. The similarity between the two candidates’ names sparked a Department of Justice (DOJ) lawsuit seeking to block the state’s election certification, citing potential voter confusion.

In a statement to The Hill, the incumbent senator’s campaign accused Peltola of “gaslighting” Alaskan voters.

“Alaskans deserve to know the truth. Mary Peltola, her campaign, and her senior advisors colluded with the DSCC [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee], national Democrat lawyers, and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit a candidate to deliberately deceive and confuse voters, and then repeatedly lied about it,” campaign spokesperson Nate Adams said. “Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along.”

A spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign did not immediately return The Hill’s request for comment.

Several GOP lawmakers, including Sen. Tim Scott (S.C.), the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, ripped Peltola over the allegations.

“Alaskans will leave Peltola unranked on the ballot because of her dirty tricks. Voters can trust the real Dan Sullivan, and I’m confident he’ll be re-elected,” Scott wrote in a post to social platform X.

“Two terms in Congress. Zero bills signed into law. But she found time to hunt down every Dan Sullivan in Alaska,” Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) wrote on X . “Let’s elect the REAL Dan Sullivan.”

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) also weighed in, claiming Peltola was involved in “a direct scheme to undermine the integrity of the election.”

The DOJ filed its lawsuit over challenger Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot last week, attempting to block certification of the election if the incumbent senator loses. Peltola sharply criticized the lawsuit , calling it “desperate” and saying she has faith in the integrity of Alaska’s elections.

“We’ve been running great elections for decades. There have never really been any abnormalities or irregularities to speak of,” Peltola said in an interview on MS NOW. “I have total confidence in Alaskans’ ability to know who they’re voting for.”

Alaska’s GOP-led state Legislature asked a federal court Monday to dismiss the DOJ’s lawsuit, following a similar motion from American Civil Liberties Union lawyers on behalf of nonprofit watchdog group Common Cause.

Trump accused Democrats of breaking the law in a post to Truth Social Wednesday afternoon.

“It has just been determined that the Democrats in Alaska illegally searched for, and recruited, a man named Dan Sullivan to run against our distinguished Republican Senator, Dan Sullivan, in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan,” Trump wrote.

articles.title: 3 battlegrounds where ticket-splitting could make the difference
articles.summary: A handful of key gubernatorial and Senate contests in battleground states could hinge on split-ticket voters as Republicans look to keep control of both offices. Split-ticket voting has dwindled in recent cycles: A Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) forecast from last week suggests an average gap of more than 6 percentage points between the Senate and…
articles.body:
A handful of key gubernatorial and Senate contests in battleground states could hinge on split-ticket voters as Republicans look to keep control of both offices.

Split-ticket voting has dwindled in recent cycles: A Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) forecast from last week suggests an average gap of more than 6 percentage points between the Senate and gubernatorial races this cycle with a median difference of 5 points — a far cry from the 28-percentage point average margin gap between the races and 25-point median difference in 1990.

Despite lower rates of ticket-splitting, the rare voters that cross party lines may prove decisive in Democrats’ hopes of a sweep on Election Day as they look to capitalize on the GOP’s bleak political outlook.

More than two dozen states are holding elections for both Senate and governor next week. Seven states — according to the analysis from DDHQ chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley last week — are most likely to see ticket-splitting: Maine, Iowa, Alaska, New Hampshire, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.

Here’s three key states The Hill’s keeping a close eye on:

One state that is almost certain to see split-ticket voting is the Granite State.

DDHQ forecasts Gov. Kelly Ayotte (R) has a 72 percent probability of winning reelection and Rep. Chris Pappas (D) has an 84 percent chance of succeeding Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D).

New Hampshire is no stranger to splitting its ticket: The state voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris, Ayotte and two Democratic House members in 2024. While former Gov. Chris Sununu, a Republican, served as the top executive of the state from 2017 to 2025, Shaheen and Sen. Maggie Hassan (D) served in the Senate during that same period.

Dante Scala, a political science professor at the University of New Hampshire, said Ayotte had the resources early on to define herself by airing advertising on largely bipartisan issues while also tying Democrat Cinde Warmington to the opioid crisis — an attack line that was used against the Democrat in her unsuccessful 2024 gubernatorial bid.

Warmington was a lobbyist for OxyContin-maker Purdue Pharma, and she also represented several people with ties to a clinic that was accused of overprescribing the opioid, according to New Hampshire Bulletin . She has said she didn’t know the dangers of the medication at the time.

“If I had known in 2001 what we all later learned, I would never, ever have done this work,” she said of her time at Purdue Pharma in a video to supporters.

Regardless, Ayotte has effectively tied this work to the Democrat, Scala argued.

“Warmington really hasn’t had the resources to reply effectively and to try to move the conversation onto something else,” Scala added.

The Senate race is more national, however, Scala said, pointing to Trump’s poor approval ratings, the state’s slight Democratic tilt and the large deficit Sununu is tasked with making up in a bleak environment for the GOP as boosting Pappas. Scala also suggested the Democrat has been “underrated” as a candidate.

“The whole congressional delegation: Shaheen, Hassan, [Democratic Rep. Maggie] Goodlander, Pappas — they’re all very comfortable in that center-left lane.” Scala said. “They might get dinged as moderates during a primary, like Pappas did, but … the New Hampshire electorate has a comfort level with these sorts of politicians.”

Democrats in Iowa are increasingly bullish about winning the governor’s mansion, with Rob Sand largely leading Republican Zach Lahn in the polls. As of Wednesday afternoon, Sand holds a 6-point lead over his opponent in DDHQ’s polling average , forecasting a 70 percent probability that the Democrat wins next week.

But flipping retiring Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst’s (R) seat may be a tougher task. Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek are neck and neck , as Hinson leads her opponent by less than half a percentage point in the latest average. DDHQ projects Hinson has a 54 percent chance of winning the seat in November.

Timothy Hagle, an associate professor of political science at the University of Iowa, said Sand may be better positioned than Lahn because of “no party” or independent voters.

These Iowans, who often make or break elections in the state, tend to like incumbents. Even though Sand is not an incumbent, he may be treated as one since he already holds statewide office and wider name recognition.

Hagle suggested Lahn has also had to work hard to introduce himself to Republican voters as a lesser known candidate than his chief primary rival, Rep. Randy Feenstra (R).

“He’s got to convince Republicans that he’s sufficiently conservative enough that they’re going to actually vote for him,” Hagle said.

In the Senate race, the professor noted Hinson has an easier leap from the House to the Senate than her rival, who serves in the state House.

“Hinson had a much better command of the details and the programs, and she can speak to specific things that she introduced into Congress,” he said of Hinson’s debate performance.

“Turek just didn’t have that,” Hagle added, noting the state lawmaker didn’t have the same record to cite.

One other state worth watching is the Buckeye State, where Democrats are looking to wrest back control of the governor’s mansion and Senate. A DDHQ forecast shows Democrat Amy Acton with a 60 percent chance of winning the governor’s race against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.

Ramaswamy’s campaign took a hit last week when it aired a controversial ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother Donna Arthur, who called her daughter “a liar” and urged voters not to support her.

Acton’s stepfather was indicted by a grand jury for sexually abusing Acton when she was a child. Acton’s brother Philip Stearns condemned the ad and said he and his sister were removed from Arthur’s care after their stepfather’s arrest. Arthur remained married to her husband until his death.

“If there was any kind of event that really changed the trajectory of the campaign, it was the Ramaswamy ad and the blowback to it,” Paul Beck, professor emeritus and academy professor of political science at Ohio State University, told The Hill.

The gubernatorial candidate and fellow Democrats denounced the ad, and some Republicans have even suggested that Ramaswamy shouldn’t have run the ad at all.

Beck suggested that controversy “really moved” the contest “out of a ‘too close to call’ contest to one in which Acton would be favored to be the winner.”

Meanwhile, the Senate race between Sen. Jon Husted (R) and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is a bit tighter, with DDHQ giving Brown a 55 percent chance of winning the seat in the upper chamber.

Ohio has trended Republican in recent years, but Brown’s name recognition in the state could push him across the finish line. Brown lost reelection to the Senate just two years ago.

But Beck chalks the tighter match-up in the Senate up to the fact that both Democrats and Republicans have aired effective attack ads.

“The Husted campaign has done a pretty good job in its ads at depicting Sherrod Brown as somebody who has been in office long enough,” Beck said, adding that the Ohio Democrat’s campaign has effectively tied the incumbent to Trump.

articles.title: Pretti family: DOJ refusing to turn over evidence
articles.summary: The parents of Alex Pretti, the Minneapolis nurse who was shot and killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year, accused the Department of Justice (DOJ) of protecting those responsible for his death and refusing to provide answers about the ongoing investigation. “At every turn, they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex’s killers,”…
articles.body:
The parents of Alex Pretti, the Minneapolis nurse who was shot and killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year, accused the Department of Justice (DOJ) of protecting those responsible for his death and refusing to provide answers about the ongoing investigation.

“At every turn, they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex’s killers,” Alex Pretti’s father, Michael Pretti, said during a news conference in Minneapolis alongside his wife, Susan. “This is not normal. It is not justice.”

Michael and Susan Pretti spoke alongside a photograph of their slain son in their first public news conference since his killing in January. The pair said they have received no communication from federal officials in the nine months since his death, despite repeatedly seeking information about the investigation.

“Share the evidence now so prosecutors can follow the facts and hold these men accountable,” Michael Pretti said. “Do your job and stop shielding Alex’s killers.”

Their attorney, Steven Schleicher, said the DOJ’s refusal to provide updates violates the federal Crime Victims’ Rights Act. In July, he sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding answers about the investigation and the identities of the agents involved, but the family says it has received no response.

The family has also criticized the Department of Homeland Security for failing to retract its initial characterization of Alex Pretti as a threat to law enforcement. Shortly after the shooting, the agency claimed he had intended to “do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement” — an account contradicted by video footage of the encounter.

“We learned about his death from the media as we saw him being shot repeatedly in the back after helping a woman from his community, a fellow Minnesotan, who had been shoved to the ground viciously,” said Michael Pretti. “No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex. No one from the federal government has called us since.”

Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, was killed Jan. 24 while filming immigration agents during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota. His death came less than three weeks after another Minneapolis resident, Renee Good, was fatally shot by a federal immigration officer, fueling protests and calls for investigations into the administration’s enforcement operations.

articles.body:
Meta, Snap head back to LA court in social media addiction trial

Social media giants Meta and Snap, the company behind Snapchat, are heading back to court this week for the latest trial in a lawsuit alleging their platforms were intentionally designed to be addictive for young users.

Jury selection began in Los Angeles Superior Court Wednesday for a case brought by two teenage plaintiffs alleging the companies’ social media platforms caused or contributed to “serious mental health injuries they suffered as adolescents.”

The bellwether case is among the thousands of claims brought against social media companies over the design of their platforms in recent years.

One of the plaintiffs, S.J., a teenager from Illinois, started using Snapchat at a young age, accessing app features like “Snapstreaks” and “Snapscore,” according to attorneys for the adolescent. S.J. also used the app’s filters and push notifications.

These features, attorneys allege, played a role in her compulsive use of Snapchat and her struggles with depression, an eating disorder, anxiety and self-harm.

Like S.J., the second plaintiff, K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, said she started using Instagram and Snapchat as a child.

Both plaintiffs also sued TikTok and YouTube but reached settlements with the platforms in the weeks ahead of the trial. Meta and S.J. also reached a settlement last week, her attorneys said.

The jury is scheduled to hear testimony from multiple tech executives, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg , Snap CEO Evan Spiegel and Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, next month.

While Spiegel has testified in high-profile congressional hearings, his expected appearance will mark the first trial testimony for the Snap CEO.

articles.body:
John E. Sununu pushed back this week against his brother’s recent suggestion that the New Hampshire Senate nominee would be “up by 30 points” if voters believed it was him on the ballot.

Former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu made the comment in an interview with CNN after the Democratic nominee in the race, Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.), suggested his opponent was purposefully omitting his first name from campaign materials to confuse voters into thinking his brother was running for Senate.

“I love my brother, but he’s totally wrong,” John Sununu said when asked by Fox News’s Paul Steinhauser about the comment Tuesday.

“This is a race that no one thought would be in play a year ago, and it’s a toss-up race right now,” he continued. “And that’s just a testament of our campaign going town to town, person to person, focusing on the right issues: bring down the cost of living, affordability, job creation.”

The former New Hampshire lawmaker is locked in a competitive Senate race against Pappas. The Cook Political Report shifted its rating in this race from a “toss-up” to favoring Democrats earlier this month after Pappas pulled ahead in the polls.

A Saint Anselm College poll released last week found the Democratic nominee pulling ahead by 7 points, while a recent GOP-sponsored National Public Affairs survey displayed a 5-point advantage for Pappas.

The GOP Senate nominee is part of the Sununu family dynasty that has long dominated politics in the Granite State.

Chris Sununu, who now serves as the president and CEO of Airlines for America, told CNN earlier this week that he was “not involved at all” in his older brother’s campaign but expressed his support for John Sununu’s Senate bid.

“We all believe in service, but you got to do it on your own,” Chris Sununu told CNN. “You got to stand on your own two feet. And I’m incredibly supportive, I’d do anything he asked me to, but he knows and I know that you’ve got to run your own race.”

articles.summary: Presented by Alliance for Aging Research {beacon} Health Care Health Care The Big Story HHS gives compounding pharmacies free rein to make certain peptides Without finalizing any new approvals or regulatory changes, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on Wednesday gave compounding pharmacies the go-ahead to make and sell six peptides lauded by…
articles.body:
HHS gives compounding pharmacies free rein to make certain peptides

Without finalizing any new approvals or regulatory changes, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on Wednesday gave compounding pharmacies the go-ahead to make and sell six peptides lauded by alternative health enthusiasts for their purported health benefits.

HHS stated in a notice that it would be practicing enforcement discretion when it came to the manufacturing and sale of the peptides BPC-157, TB-500, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c and Semax.

In its notice, the HHS acknowledged these peptides are not FDA-approved, evaluated for safety and may even “pose risks to patients,” but stated the decision by the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) indicated “significant interest” in peptide use.

Earlier this year, the PCAC voted in favor adding these peptides to the FDA’s DA’s 503A list of bulk drug substances that can be used in compounding. Prior to the meeting, FDA scientists had concluded in briefing materials that there was not enough evidence to support these peptides being safe and effective.

For a 503A compounding pharmacy to manufacture and sell a substance, the product must either meet quality standards under the United States Pharmacopeia or National Formulary monograph; be a component of an FDA-approved product; or be on the FDA’s 503A compounding list.

Pro-peptide groups welcomed the news on Wednesday.

Scott Brunner, CEO of the Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding , said in a statement, “We’ve said all along that the question isn’t whether patients are using these peptides. They are. The question is where they’re getting them. Right now, far too many patients are obtaining peptides from illicit suppliers with little assurance about what’s actually in the vial.”

Other groups like the Partnership for Safe Medicines (PSM) pushed back on the decision.

“Today’s decision leaves Americans in a grey area as to whether peptides are safe or not, even though the FDA’s own scientists recommended against voting in favor of these substances due to concerns with evidence,” PSM Executive Director Shabbir Imber Safdar said in a statement.

“Overlooked in this vote is that many newly appointed PCAC members appear to have conflicts of interest directly related to the peptide substances under consideration. This outcome shreds any sense of credibility and transparency, placing their interests above the safety of the American people,” he added.

Democrat David Crowley has slightly widened his lead over GOP nominee Tom Tiffany in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial contest , according to new polling released Wednesday.

The Marquette University Law School Poll found that Crowley increased his support among likely voters in the state by 2 percentage points from a survey last month to 51 percent in October. The Milwaukee County executive’s 7-point advantage over his GOP opponent fell within the poll’s margin of error.

Forty-four percent of likely voters in this new poll backed the former Republican U.S. House member, after Tiffany received 46 percent support in September. Four percent of voters said they were still undecided in this contest ahead of the midterm election on Tuesday.

Additionally, the Democrat’s favorability among voters rose by six percentage points since last month, while the Republican’s grew by one point.

Both candidates saw their support among independent voters grow in this latest survey. Crowley’s support from this group rose from 44 percent in September to 56 percent in October, while Tiffany’s increased from 18 percent to 26 percent in the same time frame.

Crowley and Tiffany are vying to replace retiring Gov. Tony Evers (D) in the Nov. 3 election. Recent polling has shown the Democrat with a narrow lead in this race.

The Marquette survey also found there was greater excitement among Democratic voters in the state to vote in this election — mirroring a larger enthusiasm gap among Republicans and Democrats playing out nationwide this election cycle.

Eighty-two percent of Democratic voters in this survey said they were either “very” or “somewhat” enthusiastic about casting their ballot in the midterms, compared to 74 percent of Republican voters.

The Marquette poll was conducted between Oct. 14 and 22 among 818 Wisconsin registered voters with a margin of error of approximately 4.3 percentage points. Among the survey’s 668 likely voters, the margin of error was approximately 4.7 percentage points.

articles.body:
Allegations that Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting “spoiler” candidates to siphon votes from incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan shook up the Alaska Senate race on Wednesday.

Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats denied any involvement, but Republicans responded sharply, accusing her of deliberately lying to Alaskans. President Trump accused Peltola of election interference and said she should be prosecuted.

But the strong partisan reactions may mean little to voters, many of whom have already cast their ballots, or at least made up their minds less than a week before Election Day.

The claims surfaced in a report from the New York Times on Wednesday, which found Peltola’s campaign recruited someone with the same name as her GOP opponent to also run for Senate in an effort to dilute the GOP vote.

Republicans immediately jumped on the report, hoping to make it stick as they defend Sullivan with six days to go.

“Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along,” said Nate Adams, a spokesperson for the Sullivan campaign, in a statement.

But according to some political experts and local strategists, six days is not long enough for a story like this to make an impact, and a news report from a national outlet might be less of a bombshell in the race as Republicans hope.

Aubrey Weiber, founder of the 907 Initiative, a Democratic-leaning government watchdog group in Anchorage, said he doesn’t expect voters to be moved much by the new allegations, because early voting is already underway and most voters he’s surveyed have already decided on their Senate picks.

“What we are seeing when we’re testing advertising, you know, like message testing, and just in polling for quite a while now, there are very few people that have not made up their minds,” Weiber said.

He added that he had just come out of casting his own vote at a polling place, where even a busy morning was the slowest workers had apparently seen all week.

More than 50,000 ballots have already been cast in the state, according to the Department of Elections.

Some Republicans have suggested the Peltola campaign’s moves are illegal. Trump said Peltola should be dropped from the ballot over the “election fraud.”

Scott Kendall, a longtime Republican staffer who now works as a lawyer and is unaffiliated with either campaign, called the ballot stacking scheme “a dirty trick” but clarified that it is not illegal.

State law does not have a motive qualifier for candidates, he said, meaning candidates can run regardless of their reasons for doing so.

The Peltola campaign and national Democrats noted that Republicans have also propped up “spoiler” Democratic and Green Party candidates in this cycle and in previous years, according to the Anchorage Daily News . The practice of recruiting fringe candidates to shape a ballot in favor of a frontrunner is also common in states beyond Alaska.

Steve Jarding, a Democratic consultant and former communications director for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), said it wasn’t unusual for both he and his GOP counterparts to look for spoiler candidates to put on ballots.

“When I was at the Senate committee in Washington for four years, you did stuff like that because you look for an advantage,” Jarding said. “We never would have done anything to break the law because none of us wanted to go to jail for doing something stupid. But committees recruiting candidates, they do it all the time.”

Weiber also said that a previous report from the Times about Peltola’s staff culture, which included claims that she had used slurs and otherwise mistreated staffers, had little ripple into voters’ minds.

“There was a lot of memes online for a couple days. That was about it,” Weiber said. “And really, like I haven’t heard about that in weeks.”

Polls taken both before after the staffers story broke in late September showed Peltola ahead of Sullivan.

Glenn Wright, professor of political science at the University of Alaska Southeast, similarly said he doesn’t expect character stories to substantially alter the election outcome.

Not only have gobs of money already been spent trying to characterize both candidates, but Alaska politics are personal and many voters have connections to one candidate or the other already, Wright said.

“I suspect that there are a very small number of people in Alaska who haven’t made up their mind yet,” Wright said. “I think most Alaskans have a pretty clear view at this point of who Mary Peltola is and who Dan Sullivan is.”

Kendall, the GOP lawyer, also acknowledged that voters are probably already entrenched. The governor’s race and ballot measure about ranked-choice voting are more consequential for Alaska politics than the Senate race, he noted.

“On this race, there’s a very calcified electorate,” Kendall said. “There’s numbers in the high 40s on both sides that are just sort of, they know who they’re supporting, and they are not persuaded.”

Kendall also pointed out that the state’s ranked-choice, nonpartisan electoral system, which he helped design, should mitigate any issues with voter confusion, because voters who don’t know which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent can rank both.

“If every person who doesn’t want Mary Peltola to win ranks the other three candidates, ranks all of them in any order, there’s no question; those votes will eventually go to [Sen.] Dan Sullivan,” Kendall said. “So, I mean, that’s the good news. What this whole sordid affair shows is that a system like Alaska’s is vital to protecting us from this outside meddling.”

Wright said the Peltola campaign’s alleged attempts to shape the race showed they misunderstand how ranked-choice voting works.

“I think a lot of Alaskans kind of chuckle and roll their eyes at the whole Dan Sullivan thing,” Wright said. “There’s no small number of Alaskan voters who are a little bit insulted by the implication that they can’t figure out which Dan Sullivan to vote for on the ballot.”

Caroline Vakil and Ford McCracken contributed
